Fun Stuff

Cars

Part 1. Revisiting unorthodox automotive designs

Frontal area is said to be a key factor influencing a car's aerodynamics. Sometimes there are outliers, e.g. BMW M4 GT3, but in general we assume a car with less frontal area will experience less drag if we leave everything else equal. For instance, if we sawed off the A-pillars of a Ferrari 296 GTB, lower the enclosed rooftop and let the driver take up both seats to lay down sideways, and compare it to a regular 296 GTB. The former should go faster. I believe most people would agree on that.

Venturi duct is a very debatable feature when it comes to improving aerodynamics. It is certain that in many cases venturi ducts do help increase downforce, depending on where the ducts are placed. However, it is uncertain whether they help reduce drag despite reducing frontal area. The answer is more likely negative, but I think it also depends on the structure.

The 1967 OSI Silver Fox was built with a huge center duct to break the 24hr Le Mans record, but never got effectively tested because the company went bankrupt. However, the performance of WMC250EV, also with a center duct, seems to be justified.

S-ducts are more common these days especially on hypercars. While the Lotus Evija stands out as one of the most aggressive ones, it had lower stats (top speed, cd value, etc.) compared to other hypercars around the same era despite having a shit load of downforce and 2039hp.

The conclusion here is, while the pressure difference created by s-ducts may increase downforce but worsen drag tolerance, a large enough center duct might have been beneficial for reducing drag and achieving higher top speeds, but there is a lot of work in terms of converting the structure – the main reason we don't see modern quads with this technology.

Part 2. An Automotive Design Shortcut?

The most widely recognized procedure for developing automotive concepts is to start from sketches. Some rare examples in history are seen using scale models ONLY and no sketches at all… and eventually they get to make a fully-functional prototype. E.g. Lotec Sirius.

For a overly-modeling-skewed person with minimal professional sketching experience, a proposed approach can be as follows:

  • Build-from-scratch a physical model
  • Scan it into a digital 3d model
  • Adjust for size & mirroring (if necessary)
  • 3D print & hands-on modifications
  • Have specialists render, engineer, and test on it.
  • Repeat process 1–5 until maximum satisfactory

If building-from-scratch (Example 2) was tedious, we can start from an existing bodywork that has the overall best-fit structure (matching wheel-bases). See the conversion from Ferrari 488 GTB to a Touring Superleggera Arese RH-95 in Example 1 (The real ones were also converted from 488 donor cars):

*As of Fall 2023 both techniques still outperform advanced prototyping on the DIY market by a few indicators, but is highly dependent on personal skills.

The fastest camera car reimagined

At some point, Koenigsegg decided that the sensible way to film record-breaking runs was to turn a Regera into a camera car, which also meant that the Huracam quietly lost its title as the fastest camera car in the world. The rig hanging off the Regera however is not the most aerodynamic object ever attached to a hypercar and probably introduces exactly the kind of turbulence one normally spends millions trying to remove, but perhaps enough horsepower is all you need. The team behind the Yangwang U9 Xtreme later arrived at roughly the same conclusion.

Anyway, if we are already committed to this level of nonsense, we might as well make the camera system look as though somebody cared about aerodynamics!

KACS Unit 1 is basically an aerodynamic frame carrying a single robotic arm, with a compact PTZ camera suspended underneath. The frame uses a specially designed targa section and extends rearward over the engine cover, giving it something vaguely resembling a One:1 rear-wing structure rather than a film set ‘accidentally welded’ onto a Regera. The camera can sweep through roughly 270 degrees, although the car itself still blocks much of the forward view, meaning the system is naturally better at filming things beside it than directly ahead. If maximum coverage matters more than airflow, the camera can instead sit on top of the frame, removing most of the structure from its line of sight at the cost of some aerodynamic dignity.

← Richard W.

July 2, 2026

Anyone who uses/expects/promotes whatever AI soulmate type product for whatever purpose is an absolute 3D (delusional, dystopian, degenerate) loser and should be condemned.

Addressing taste issues in quality prototyping

In recent years, China has continued to pull ahead of the US in physical prototyping and manufacturing, not just in cost and scale, which everyone already expects. The growing number of small businesses that combine quality, speed, and tolerance for messy requests has made idea-to-refined services flourish outside the enterprise level. Since 2020, anyone can start a capable DIY studio in China with minimal capital and relatively little training. The US lacks a sufficiently dense ecosystem of such serious small-scale production because demand for high-quality execution remains limited, which is firsthand subject to high-quality resources being generally expensive and hard to access. While the usual explanations regarding labor costs, supply-chain gaps, factory shortages, and real-world operational friction are all relevant, the demand side, and typically the fact that the market itself trains what is possible is often less talked about: Customers who accept mediocre finishes and creators who reward suppliers primarily on cost have started to reveal a missing contingency buffer between the sudden technological improvements and supposedly improved demand standards. This became particularly obvious when the US imported the same machines and materials, yet still failed to import the habits that produce good results at scale.

One way to illustrate this is to look at the figurine boom from 2024 to early 2026 when considerable attention went toward AI tools for 3D generation. Figurines quickly became the main object type produced by new tools due to being simple-enough manufacturable products that didn’t require much consideration regarding functions or durability other than aesthetic taste. Tripo, Meshy, and similar tools could turn a prompt into a 3D asset, while better desktop machines like the Makera Z1 made the factory look as if it had been miniaturized onto a desk. For a while, this promise was real in the limited sense that demos are real: the interval between an idea and visible geometry had collapsed. Then many outsiders realized that an overall geometry is only the beginning of the process: Despite it becoming easy to sell the illusion that the distance from vision to implementation has become visibly short, none of these tools could address more than a single-stage workflow without solving the system surrounding it: The persistent difficulties of assembly logic, tolerances, material behavior, surface finishing, durability, repeatability, and real-world trial and error that needed to be solved all the time.

And even having learned all that, mass-produced artifacts through AI-embedded workflows were missing the reasons to be made more than once, i.e., the answers lying in the art of business and branding, something that the technically skewed minds couldn’t learn easily. The cooling hype of the figurine boom hardly affected experienced practitioners, as many would have either used AI workflows selectively or never switched to 3D AI workflows, presumably due to such workflows hardly outcompeting in indicators other than speed compared to traditional resin castings.

Solution

The US market for quality prototyping for independent creators being oppressive due to taste issues is gradually being solved as emerging companies improve and expand their product ecosystems. But further steps could revolve around switching from broad narratives to facilitating differentiated, specific, branded, superior products. More detailed directions may include:

  • Tools perfecting the idea-to-refined loop
  • E.g. 1. Open-source rapid workflows for assembly logic; 2. Physical AI that understands when to switch between different procedures & techniques to ensure optimal output. Both are especially difficult to do at scale using current AI software. As of Jul 2026, Tripo AI segmentation v2 almost handles the assembly basics in digital form, but is yet to see effectiveness in real-world production.
  • Entirely new distribution channels and branding
  • Use advanced production methods to create objects that cannot be reproduced easily with average equipment. These capabilities should be supported by distinctive products, strong branding, and new distribution channels.
  • Engineer equipment around product vision
  • Instead of building isolated machines that complete only one stage of production, engineer systems around a coherent product and brand strategy.
Dogma

There are a handful of things to be very careful about. But instead of showing a list, I’ll address a variety of things I’ve seen and experienced firsthand.

The topic I would like to start with is navigating purpose.

“Purpose” is among the most grounded, widely discussed, but easily confused ideas in modern life. You especially do not want to misunderstand it in startups, because once you do, everyone involved begins paying for the confusion. One way to see the problem is to notice how many failures are better explained by purpose than by skill, and how “purpose matters more than skills” survives mostly as a motivational slogan while being practiced far less often in reality; some of this has to do with people making excuses for weak self-accountability, prestige-whoring, and being distracted all the time. But a less discussed problem is how hard it can be for certain people, including many capable ones, to distinguish purpose from the systems that happen to reward them; they think it ‘takes them lots of time’ and other things. I became increasingly curious about how all this confusion was going on, comparing my observations while in the US from 2002-2011, China from 2011 to 2021, and then the US again from 2021 till now.

Some groups appear especially vulnerable to this confusion. They try so hard to do three things: 1. Constantly stressing about their own lack of purpose but with minimal forward-looking intent; 2. Relying on external people/systems, preferably the most credible ones available to them, to help them “discover” what they should do; and then 3. Mistaking that externally assigned direction for the actual reason they are doing it, only to blame the system once the rewards stop arriving at their expectation. Some third-culture IELTS tutors probably have a story or two about this. You can observe versions of this at nearly every economic class and stage of life. In some sense, it is related to the degree to which a society organizes important functions around unified, top-down, easily legible metrics, and such metrics easily become counterfeit purpose for the average individual.

  • Exhibit 1. While a fair reason for Gen Zs to go study abroad is that a highly centralized education system with a large systemic obsession with grades and rankings was too painful for them to endure1, little do they realize the metric-obsessive mentality which they themselves possess will bother them all along, whether they admit it or not. The discussion of university rankings lasting late into our 30s has shown how hard it is to change this mentality. Such fears were further borne out in recent years, when today’s graduates from even highly ranked universities encounter a labor market being rearranged by technology. Older generations can also miss this point when they wonder why children they pushed so aggressively toward measurable success seem strangely unhappy, passive, or lost afterward.
  • Exhibit 2. Many of us who attended American universities have seen arguments over grade curves, publication pressure, and administrative incentives, but those can still look mild compared with institutions elsewhere where minimum graduation or pass-rate expectations are effectively imposed from above and instructors are left to to ‘figure it out’, sometimes through practices that would plainly be called fraud if the metric itself had not first been granted institutional legitimacy.2
  • Exhibit 3. Some companies, including certain automakers, mass-produce consumer products largely to overtake competitors across a respectable-looking list of metrics, but end up dismissed by the market as sacrificing reliability and basic safety for performance, because the metrics replace the purpose rather than serve it; meanwhile, the ThrustSSC being the fastest ground vehicle on earth is successful precisely because its narrow metric followed from its purpose.

Metrics matter in many senses, and a metric-obsessive mentality is not necessarily fatal; for people with genuinely critical judgment, its pros and cons can often be navigated, and it will be interesting to see how far things develop. But a serious concern may be how much we underestimate its growth in Silicon Valley today, until we repeatedly encounter the kind of opportunistic founders who infer the size of an opportunity simply from the popularity of a topic—say, the number of talks, research proposals, or posts about it on X—yet have almost nothing to say about something that appears important and technically interesting simply because the visible market looks small! My stance is that you neither want metrics to be the priority consideration for a serious purpose, nor the sole factor dictating purpose, especially when starting companies.

Opportunists3

Being opportunistic on certain occasions, I never saw Artificial Intelligence creating a large group of opportunists as the real issue. Instead, we should really be concerned 4about how this era is creating the worst opportunist types ever: Opportunists who don’t admit, and opportunists who trick both others and themselves. It will only get worse as lack of self-realization and an obsession with metrics-based judgement grow among young people.

Metrics and Judgement

Without a clear purpose, judgment loses its standard, so people retreat to metrics as substitutes for knowing what actually matters. Some know to what degree they should judge based on indicators/metrics. But it is crucial to understand that data sets by their very nature are backward-looking, and creativity by its very nature is forward-looking. An illustration of this is how observers who judge on failed company cases think they’ve mastered how NOT to run a company, but only find out how different realities are when they become the operators building one themselves, especially if they were given the same idea or problem. The distinction is not whether operators have more information than observers, but operators are forced to recover first principles and define what success means under real dynamic constraints, while observers can avoid that responsibility and judge through whatever indicators are easiest to see. We are all, more or less, armchair experts in various periods of our lives; while we are constantly learning to move beyond that, choosing to be a ‘supposedly smart’ but backward-looking person in a forward-looking industry can be one of the worst life choices a person can make.

Metrics can be very misleading. But today’s generation tend to base their judgment on metrics more than they realize, thinking metrics can lead to more certainty but only to cause more noise. In a niche sense, you might not want to use startdowns.ai to determine real company potential, especially during broad hostility toward “AI slop,”5 since startups systematically getting more downvotes may cause a high likelihood of some good companies being misinterpreted or mistaken. See how the uncertainties magnify when it comes to many companies being built supposedly based on nonconsensus truths; however, they can be solved or seriously examined by operators through deep learning and sustained focus.

Clarity of purpose is what makes deep study and sustained focus effective enough to turn an outsider into an insider6, or a generalist into a better specialist and, eventually a better generalist again. The current obsession with LLMs, however, has made it unusually easy to move across many subjects quickly enough to feel informed without remaining anywhere long enough to become so. That makes this a useful moment for self-examination, no matter how well we think we understand the models themselves. The broader AI panic may ultimately make this point more convincingly than any call-to-action from a neurodivergent AuDHD person who has gone through several lessons.

Unlike LLMs, which can process certain categories of work in parallel with little apparent cost, humans eventually reach a point where multitasking produces diminishing and then negative returns. Beyond that threshold, breadth begins to work against insider knowledge, original judgment, and real innovation; when generalists without specialist depth repeatedly discover ideas that have existed for decades and briefly mistake rediscovery for invention, the result is not evidence that we have become unusually creative, but shows how shallow generalization can produce a dangerous feeling of completion before we have stayed with a problem long enough to discover any secrets.

The AI Panic in the job market

By now we have accumulated plenty of reasons to doubt the simple story that LLMs are replacing humans wholesale, while many recent layoffs appear at least as connected to cost structures and policy adjustments as to technological displacement itself. Yet this has done little to reverse a mentality among young college kids that the safest response to uncertainty is to multitask and grasp as many opportunities as possible. The irony here is that this supposed risk reduction can make people more replaceable, while an insider who stays deeply focused on one problem at a time will usually discover far more work that AI cannot easily perform, either because it requires judgment, context, taste, trust, physical interaction… things that only become visible after prolonged exposure. From there, the choice is fairly open: exploit the human advantage directly, help build better applications of AI around what you have learned, join a mature company where that depth matters, or start something with the right people.

Now let us return to the purpose question: Why start a company? Two common answers today are that “now is the best time to start”—usually some mixture of technological optimism and FOMO—and that building a company is one of the fastest ways to do something impressive enough to “differentiate yourself from everyone else”. Neither answer is necessarily wrong under the current technological landscape; both can even be rational. But what have we done when they stop being secondary considerations and quietly become the reason?

We are living through an unusually favorable period for starting companies, but perhaps also an unusually favorable period for wanting to be a founder without wanting anything specific badly enough to justify founding one: The prestige hierarchy that once concentrated around universities, consulting firms, banks, and large tech companies has long migrated into entrepreneurship and has seen considerable growth under the influence of the advancements of Artificial Intelligence. This helps explain several strange tendencies in the current startup ecosystem.

  • A large number of companies now fall into the “shovel seller” category, to the point that shovel-selling has formed an over-invested loop of its own, reaching ever higher valuations while solving remarkably little outside the ecosystem that created the demand for those shovels in the first place.
  • Automation has become too easy, making it increasingly common to confuse “this can now be automated” with “this deserves to become a company.” And with that ease comes one of the lazier confusions of the current startup cycle: that because a workflow can be automated, the workflow itself must have been the problem, which is simply false in many industries! Take real estate rental as an example, where stakeholders’ responsibilities and systems were never designed to share state or coordinate cleanly through the digital infrastructure now sitting on top of them, and thus automating one visible step may save several minutes while leaving the actual coordination failure almost untouched.7
  • One increasingly common form of prestige-whoring is the founder wannabe who says he wants to start a company primarily because he wants to “do his own thing,” “work for himself,” or become independent, which is almost delusional. The desire for independence without an appetite for responsibility is not entrepreneurial independence at all, but the fantasy of authority without obligation, made especially attractive to a generation that has grown up too comfortable and told for years that personal freedom means minimizing the number of things one owes to other people.
  • Since technology has become so capable, it is now fashionable to insist that startups begin with the smallest team possible, because small teams supposedly move faster—as they say. Perhaps; but a market full of tiny, fragmented teams also happens to be ideal for the giants, which can let them absorb risk, test markets, and build around their platforms before buying, copying, hiring, or crushing whatever proves useful. Eventually you get a thousand small teams that may look like decentralization from below and consolidation from above. The waves of startups being erased by each major OpenAI release are less a demonstration that startups are doomed than a reminder that speed is not defensibility, and technological dependency is not technological depth. While many young founders appear to know this in theory, they continue to build companies that assume the opposite in practice.
  • Technical prestige whoring is how a large part of today’s tech founders constantly chase whatever appears technically impressive, until they discover halfway through that conventional business experience has taught them little about how capital, incentives, institutions, and public adoption actually interact; this is one way of showing some of today’s young tech founders not learning & practicing enough economics, although they may seem forward-looking. Young tech founders also overlook the fact that the more widely available a capability becomes, the less distinction comes from merely possessing it: At this very moment in history, AI chatbots aren’t inherently interesting since Q3 2025. The same thing is happening to AI agents now.

As these ego-empowering cycles grow, it also happens to work remarkably well for the tech giants: opportunists enter startups during a boom, build on top of infrastructure owned by increasingly powerful companies, and, once their own projects go bust, often return as better-credentialed employees. No elaborate conspiracy is necessary, and forget customer feedback loops—this may be one of the most interesting loops (or rigs, I would call) Gen Z gets to watch operate and contribute to in real time!

While it is easy to blame tech giants, investors, accelerators, or startup culture for this, it is probably more useful to reconsider our own definition of purpose, or simply why we do things at all.

We have heard often enough that purpose should not be treated as an object hidden somewhere inside the self, waiting to be discovered through sufficient introspection; the suggestion earlier is to take a position, attach to something concrete, and remain there long enough for the shallow reasons to wear off. Perhaps serious purpose is not especially mystical. Someone may encounter something so inefficient or painful that ignoring it starts to feel more irrational than trying to fix it, and just happen to start a company, similar to how people into trading might turn out to be less miserable by autosuggesting they are purely passionate about it, instead of spending ten years treating it as a temporary instrument for becoming rich enough to finally start the company that will supposedly make him independent.

Altering prejudice may be a solid purpose that comes from deeper within the heart despite it being extremely challenging. One upside of being a responsible founder is we can build defensible companies that attract attention, change incentives, and make previously unrealistic technologies more economically and politically possible. But only after these purpose questions are reasonably clear does it make sense to talk seriously about paths, leverage, and what we actually want or how we want to impact the lives of others. This reminds us of the old inscription Cliff Stoll once recalled: http://www.donath.org/Quotes/AllTruthIsOne/

A note on why I don’t show a solid list: Similar to metrics, checklists might fail despite being correct. Over time I have developed a fairly strict set of things founders should not compromise on when choosing anyone whose decisions will materially affect the company; most of them concern values and principles rather than technical capability, which is usually much easier to diligence. One interesting problem is not only how strictly one should follow such a list, but also whether it should be made explicit at all, because a large part of today’s observers, including some very smart ones who possess little of it, will quickly learn to game the system either intentionally or unintentionally, and you’ll soon be fucked. So the list is useful, but mostly as a private reference against behavior over time. Someone you have watched across ten years may tell you more about human nature than some psychology courses ever will.
